ai.definition: Space tourism involves civilian passengers traveling to suborbital or orbital space for recreational purposes. It typically includes brief exposure to microgravity and a view of the Earth's curvature.
ai.howItWorks: Passengers board spacecraft that reach altitudes above the atmosphere, providing a few minutes of weightlessness followed by re-entry into Earth's atmosphere. The experience is facilitated through private companies offering suborbital or orbital flights.
ai.problemSolved: Addresses the desire for space travel experiences and democratizes access to space beyond scientific and military endeavors.
ai.manufacturing: Spacecraft are manufactured using advanced materials and technologies, often involving custom-built rockets and capsules. Production involves high precision and rigorous testing.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes design, material selection, component manufacturing, assembly, and extensive testing phases before operational flights.
ai.costDrivers: High initial investment in R&D, specialized materials, and stringent safety standards. Operational costs include fuel, crew training, and insurance.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Expected to grow as technology matures and more companies enter the market, potentially leading to broader adoption and lower costs over time.
ai.regulation: Subject to regulatory oversight by space agencies like NASA or FAA in the U.S., ensuring safety and operational standards are met. International regulations also apply.
ai.risks: Safety risks due to the complexity of space travel, financial risks related to high initial investments and potential low passenger numbers, and environmental risks associated with rocket launches.
ai.profitability: Currently limited by high costs and small market size but expected to improve as more companies enter the market and operational efficiency increases.
ai.futureDevelopment: Potential for expanded services such as space hotels or longer-duration space flights. Technological advancements could reduce costs and increase accessibility.

glossary.def: A spaceflight that reaches an altitude above the atmosphere but does not achieve orbit, typically providing a few minutes of weightlessness and views of Earth.
A spaceflight that achieves orbit around Earth, offering extended periods in microgravity and more comprehensive views of the planet.

subsystems.name: Propulsion
subsystems.role: lifts the vehicle above the Kármán line (100 km) and controls descent.

subsystems.name: Crew capsule
subsystems.role: pressurised cabin for passengers and crew.

subsystems.name: Reusable booster
subsystems.role: carries the capsule and lands vertically for reuse.

subsystems.name: Avionics and guidance
subsystems.role: flies the trajectory and manages abort modes.

subsystems.name: Passenger systems
subsystems.role: keeps untrained passengers safe and comfortable.

buildSteps.title: Design the vehicle
buildSteps.detail: Define the trajectory (suborbital or orbital), passenger capacity and safety margins, including abort scenarios.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the structure
buildSteps.detail: Build lightweight propellant tanks and a pressurised capsule from aluminium-lithium alloys or composites.

buildSteps.title: Integrate propulsion
buildSteps.detail: Install rocket engines and plumb propellant lines, then test-fire on a stand.

buildSteps.title: Install life support and avionics
buildSteps.detail: Fit cabin environmental control, seats, windows and flight computers with redundant systems.

buildSteps.title: Test uncrewed
buildSteps.detail: Fly the full profile without passengers, including abort tests, to validate all systems.

buildSteps.title: Test with crew
buildSteps.detail: Fly company test pilots to prove the vehicle and refine procedures.

buildSteps.title: Begin commercial flights
buildSteps.detail: After regulatory approval (e.g. FAA licence), fly paying passengers on short suborbital hops or orbital stays.

buildSteps.title: Refurbish and reuse
buildSteps.detail: Recover, inspect and re-fly the vehicle, turning spaceflight into a repeatable operation rather than a one-off.

prerequisites.why: vertical take-off and landing, or air-launch, allows many flights per vehicle.
passengers need breathable air, temperature control and protection during ascent and re-entry.

prerequisites.tech: Autonomous flight control and abort systems
prerequisites.why: passengers are not pilots, so the vehicle must fly itself and escape emergencies automatically.
effects of acceleration, microgravity and radiation on untrained people are still being studied.
rules for passenger safety and informed consent vary and are still maturing.

pathway.milestone: suborbital flights by Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic
pathway.unlocks: minutes of weightlessness and a view of Earth for paying customers.

pathway.milestone: orbital tourism on Crew Dragon and future capsules
pathway.unlocks: days in orbit, including stays on commercial space stations.

pathway.milestone: commercial space stations in low Earth orbit
pathway.unlocks: regular orbital destinations, research and tourism.
very fast intercontinental journeys, if cost and safety allow.
